entry.title: Slacking as Self-Care
entry.content:
So this one time I was at a job interview at a supermarket chain based out of Welwyn Garden City and I was asked “what would you say is your biggest flaw?” Or something like that. What sticks out in memory is how cheap the office was furnished for a company which amounted to a 1 pound in every eight spent in the UK. The excuse they gave was that everything they did was ‘for the customer’ and no frills were spent on staff. Anyway, I was canny enough to understand that you don’t say something like “I’m a cold-hearted bastard” or “I’m on medication for anxiety” or “I collapse under pressure.” I realised that you’re supposed to say something which is a strength and instead make it look like a flaw. So I said that I’m a perfectionist and that everything has to be correct and that I really couldn’t even sleep if I thought I’d done a bad job. The interviewer - someone from HR - smiled in a way which is now reminiscent of an expert hunter and we moved on.

I didn’t get that job - the feedback I received was that I was too quiet in group settings - and looking back I think I gave the wrong answer. There is no correct answer to that question but saying I’m a perfectionist leaves a bad taste in my mouth. Perfectionism is a terrible flaw. You will waste your life on tasks which don’t matter. The standard cultural story is that a perfectionist is somebody who gets everything done to an impossibly high standard. Now I see why the HR rep smiled in the way she did: My desire for professional competence created a psychological trap which made me exploitable. It took me a decade to realise that some professionalism was not killing myself over every detail. Professionalism is ruthlessly distinguishing when what deserves excellence from what should be just good enough.

In other words I had to learn that to prioritise.

This meant refusing to do tasks which are neither important or urgent. I had to carry the attitude that it’s not an issue if, on a cosmic scale, things aren’t perfect. What happened is that I got much more done, and had a better time doing it, if I let my standards slip.

I can almost hear the objections: isn’t this slacking? Isn’t it selfish? Don’t you feel, even a little bit, guilty? Let me address these one by one. Yes, saying no to unimportant tasks, doing an acceptable job, this is slacking. Yes, I agree that slacking can be a bit selfish, but I disagree that it’s a vice. I would be selfish if I forced my colleagues to do pointless work, where instead I expect them to slack early and slack often. This way I sleep soundly at night.

What changed? What cured me was plotting my life out in a grid: one box for each week in a year, five years aligned vertically, each row a 52 box row. I realised that my life was finite. I coloured in the boxes that had already passed, and the empty boxes were going to get filled in whether I liked it or not. So instead of orienting myself around what I could do, or what I ought to do; instead there was what I wanted to do, and I had to chase after that.

Realising you have to prioritise isn’t sufficient. Finitude isn’t a shield against the daily stream of tasks coming your way: you still have to figure out which tasks you can refuse without consequence. So you need to classify them in some way. Classification will allow us to prioritise, and then simply drop things which aren’t a priority. It’ll also give us some idea of what slacking actually is, in a technical sense. There are millions of classification systems out there, hidden away in productivity blogs and on youtube and tiktok. By far the most popular is the Eisenhower Matrix. It’s popular because it’s simple. You might think that because the framework is simple, everyone can understand it. This is false. The idea is too simple, and easily dismissed. I have seen seasoned professionals fail not because they don’t know the Eisenhower Matrix, but because they know it and still can’t execute it. Here’s why.

The Eisenhower Matrix classifies tasks in two dimensions: Urgent and Important. Urgency implies an upcoming deadline, and a failure to complete the task in time will result in consequences. For example, if you don’t pay your rent on the 1st of the month every month, then you will get evicted. There are actual consequences attached to the deadline of an Urgent task. Actual is the operative word here, since most professionals operate in a world of fantasy consequences. You can tell that there are no consequences attached to a task because when questioned people will use language like ‘could’ ‘maybe’ ‘if’ ‘possibly’ etc. That is, completing the task will block off some hypothetical consequence in the completer’s mind, which is another way of saying that the productivity was all about anxiety or ego or something else and not anything which we can point to as a consequence collectively.

Important tasks are tasks which, in some small way, contribute to your long term goals. Maybe it’s buying a house, getting a promotion, starting a business, etc. They are about life values and long term goals. They are the raw material of what our life becomes. These are tasks that grow businesses and write books and plant orchards. They are not dotting every i and crossing every t.

So what do you do with your tasks?

First you classify them. The easiest is whether they are Urgent or not. This should be simple, since there either is, or isn’t, a deadline attached to the task. Then you decide if a task is Important. This is a little more subjective, but you can always change your mind.

Once you have your tasks classified, then there are four basic actions you need to take.

For tasks which are both Urgent and Important you need to do them now. As in, now this minute, this day, this week. These absolutely cannot wait.

Tasks which are Important but not Urgent do in your diary. You have to make a commitment to actually do them, and the strength of your commitment will determine your outcomes. The more a business owner works on their business instead of in it – for example by expanding their product range instead of serving customers the products they already have – the more that business will grow. These are your golden tickets to a different life essentially. Spending a Saturday morning drafting this, and then editing and publishing this post, this is my Important not Urgent task.

For tasks which are Urgent but not Important you need to Delegate. These are usually tasks you don’t have the expertise for. think back office functions like taxes and payroll. These need to be done, but ideally not by you since they are a distraction from your values and long term goals. These tasks are where you need to expand your team and work collaboratively. Don’t underestimate the power of being nice to people who complete these tasks.

Tasks which are neither Important or Urgent you should delete from your list. This is the most impactful lesson of the Eisenhower Matrix. I see a lot of professionals diligently prioritising their todo lists and then trying to do everything they wrote down. that’s a mistake: if something isn’t a priority, then you never do it. Simple as. There is only so much time we have in life, our attention is finite, so why waste effort on things which aren’t a priority?s

Smart people fail because their perfectionism convinces them that everything is important and urgent all at once. Every detail matters. Every task could have consequences. The framework is useless if you can’t see that most of your tasks aren’t actually priorities.

The HR rep in my interview was smiling because she’d found the perfect prey: someone who would grind himself down on every task, and blame himself for failure. A decade more experienced I know I can slack on the right things. I know those boxes will fill up anyway, just with other people’s priorities.

entry.title: Why do we suddenly all wear jeans now?

link.title: Why do we suddenly all wear jeans now?

entry.content:
Three men walk along a country road. It’s early evening, the light is clear and perfect for photography. They gaze self-assuredly at the cameraman. The gentleman on the left has a touch of unkempt hair, a cigarette dangles from his lips. All have a straight backed posture. This photograph—Young Farmers—was taken in 1914 by August Sander, and the men are off to a country dance. Incongruous with the title, each wears a hat, a suit, and carries a walking stick. In Sander’s portraits of early 20th century Germany, the pattern repeats: farmers and artisans, scholars and lawyers, most choose a two-piece woolen suit. A man in specialized workwear—a chore shirt, an overall—marked themselves as someone who couldn’t afford a suit. Today, we see the reverse: the suit is the costume. Why did this happen?

Like everything else in the world, from countries to concepts, the suit has an origin story. They originated in the late Victorian period as a reaction to the sartorial trend of the day: the morning coat. Today, mostly in deepest England, you might see a man wearing a morning coat on his wedding day, but otherwise they are reserved for the most formal of occasions. Suits, or lounge suits, as they were known, were a casual item of clothing, to be worn in the lounge (if the suit was wool) or in the countryside (if the suit was tweed). It was only later, in the early 20th century, when a suit became the choice for men. As it faded from the height of its power, the suit became the choice for the men who controlled the British Empire: the business leaders, politicians, and members of the Civil Service. The suit was the ideal clothing for deliberation, calculation, and administration. It was made of fabric that draped and moved with the body; it was easy to move about in; it did not encumber its bearer; it got out of the way, yet still retained a little of the casual respectability of London Clubs where it had long reigned. In other words, the suit was the costume of power.

Denim was, as a material, invented to solve a different problem: French workers needed cheap and durable workwear. That’s why cotton was chosen over wool. It could be woven into both soft and durable fabrics. It could be easily repaired. And it was cheap. Perfect for the poorer classes to wear daily. It became an American staple when Jacob Davis and Levi Strauss added copper rivets. These reinforced the stress points—pockets, seams—that would otherwise tear. Denim workwear then became the costume of men who built things. Primarily in the American imagination, they built the American West. It took the countercultures of the 1960s and ‘70s—rejecting the suit as a symbol of corporate conformity—to begin denim’s transformation. By the 1980s and ‘90s, Silicon Valley had completed it: tech founders wore jeans not despite their association with manual labor, but because of it. They were builders, not bureaucrats. The rest of us followed. Whilst wearing a suit marks a man out as an administrator of another man’s empires, in the 21st century denim is the costume of a certain kind of agency.

The real subject of this essay is agency. Tech founders adopted the costume of builders while becoming further removed from actual production than the suited administrators they replaced. The miner in denim jeans did build things. The CEO in designer denim at a product launch doesn’t. The 19th-century miner who wore denim actually extracted ore. The 21st-century founder who wears it… deploys capital and manages teams. The costume of building has been adopted by a class whose work is, once again, calculation and deliberation—just rebranded as ‘disruption.’ When we venerate agency as an unqualified good, we should ask: agency to do what? The suit signaled the authority to think before acting. Denim now signals the authority to act without thinking. Both extremes miss the mark. We need deliberation and execution—not just the costume of either.

entry.title: Project Management is better in Docs

link.title: Project Management is better in Docs

entry.content:
My company spends over a million Euros annually on project management software that nobody actually uses.

It’s worse than that: we actually had two pieces of software for project management, and a team that I’m part of had to transition from one usable project management software (Asana) to one that’s essentially unusable (Jira). The reasons were basically the same as any other dumb decision in tech: that everyone else also uses Jira in the organisation; that we, one plucky band of renegades, were the last holdouts globally not to use Jira, so it was difficult for people to collaborate with us; that we were costing the company north of a million euro a year for our Asana licence, and would we just move already; and that we could have enhanced help from the IT management team if we agreed on a bulk move. In fact, the IT team would dedicate us a special person to do the move so that we didn’t have to stop working; one day we’d come into the office, and we’d just find everything in Jira, it would all work, we’d have walked into the light and the golden sunshine of Collaborative Project Management.

We were bullied into moving from something we liked to something that everyone hates using; and for reasons which have nothing to do with our productivity or preferences or anything subjective and squishy like that.

But it’s even worse than that!

Even though we prefer Asana to Jira—and even that comparison is invidious, because both pieces of software are terrible—most of our project management happens in Google Docs.

It’s really simple. All of my meetings are a bunch of people staring at a Google Doc that someone is sharing live on the Big Screen in the meeting room. On the doc will be today’s date. We discuss where we’re at with things, make some notes of what we’re saying underneath today’s date, and then we assign some tasks directly in the doc to whoever is going to do the task. To labour the point a little: we’re using Google Docs, an essentially free piece of software, despite having a million euro licence for a dedicated project management software that can do far more than ‘just text.’

I’m sure if we were a Microsoft house then all of our project management would happen in Word; and I’m sure if where I worked was artsier or scrappier or whatever we’d use something like Coda or Notion or whatever the cool kids are using.

Actually, no. Neither Coda or Notion have the exact right feature, which is just a blank page and the ability to write three things:

  1. Dates
  2. Text
  3. Tasks

With the optional functionality of tagging people on the tasks they’ve been assigned. So we’d use Google Docs or Microsoft Word or Libra Office Online. We’d use them because this is the absolute best project management software, for the simple reason that all you need for project management are tasks, notes, and dates.

Surely, project management couldn’t be this simple, why does this barebones setup work?

A project is a series of tasks with a deadline. Any sort of system which marries tasks with deadlines is a workable system. It works great for individuals. Add on a feature where you can tag people on their tasks and you’ve got a system fit for teams. Google docs will suffice for that.

But we don’t just have tasks on a project, there’s also meetings—which, if you are sufficiently cognizant of the fact that in the future you will need some kind of guidance—which generate notes. It’s vital to keep your notes right next to your tasks. Notes are the context for the task, so they live together. The more context you create, the easier it will be for you when you come to do the task. The thing is, when confronted with a single line—I mean sometimes it’s just a noun— description for a task, it’s really helpful to have something, anything, around which gives context to whatever it is you’ve now got to do. Even a few bullet points is better than blank space in jogging your memory. Taking notes also means that you’re paying attention, and not, say, using your phone to catch up with the news..

The other thing docs does well is limit the amount of stuff you capture. Task managers like Todoist or Things 3 let you have essentially infinite tasks. Sure, they have complicated systems to surface the things you need when you need them; but the problem is a task you maybe created three years ago no longer speaks to you. A google doc only lets you capture so much, otherwise you have to spin out a new google doc. That is, docs encourage finitude and brevity. It’s why bullet journals are so popular: you only commit to doing so much in any given slice of time, and you only note down what you need to note down.

This way of working is the polar opposite of something like Jira, with it’s infinite backlogs and difficult to find substasks.

And we’re not the only team!

Every team in my company manages at least some of their projects in Google docs. Especially those projects that involve another team: it’s just easier to spin up a doc than it is to create a Jira board for a single short lived thing. Talking to people who work in other companies–whether in Tech, or some other industry which requires people to be in offices, but which as at best vague requirements for getting work done—they all use some version of ‘a big document with all our notes and tasks arranged by date’ as the unofficial method of project management.

So it begs the question: why do companies even bother with Jira licences, if nobody actually uses them? The answer is simple, if depressing: Jira (and other software like them) reports statistics on who did what and when. Every year my company (and basically every other company on earth) sets out a kind of Socialist Plan, setting Key Results (KRs) which it needs to hit to achieve its long term goals (set out, I kid you not, in a Five Year Plan). These KRs can be things like “reduce costs by 3%” or “fix this broken business process.” (I just illustrate here, they are not our actual KRs). Then we measure our progress against the KRs with Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), which often seem like they’re pulled from Satan’s backside. The whole company has company wide KPIs, each function has KPIs, each department in each function has KPIs, and each team in each department has KPIs. All these numbers flow together in a massive KPI tree letting every employee know how their work contributes to the entire company’s performance. So we can see why Jira, or some other software, is mandatory: with Jira’s reporting functions, the company can tie individual contributions to projects and projects to KPIs which flow all the way up from single teams to the company’s overall performance. This is all another way of saying that it’s more important that the company measure productivity, even with ass backwards tools like Jira, than it is for its employees to be actually productive.

The upshot of all of this is that you only need one thing to be productive: a place where all of the context for your projects to live alongside the tasks you have to do, and the dates those tasks are due. Google docs (or Apple notes or Microsoft Word) works just as well as anything else. The moral is that you shouldn’t sweat the organisational stuff, that should be a light scaffold over the important thing, which is that you’ve actually got to sit down and do the work.
entry.summary: My company spends over a million Euros annually on project management software that nobody actually uses.

entry.title: You cannot simply ‘change your beliefs’ to become successful.

link.title: You cannot simply ‘change your beliefs’ to become successful.

entry.content:
Nir Eyal, international bestselling author of Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products and Indistractable: How to Control Your Attention and Choose Your Life is promoting a new book Beyond Belief: Change Your Mind. Change Your Life. I attended a short zoom session via Ali Abdaal today, and honestly I just couldn’t stand it: if the zoom session is anything to go by, this book will be unconvincing. (However, this didn’t stop me from pre-ordering and, likely, hate reading the book).

The thesis of the book is: what stands between you and success is your beliefs. Change your beliefs and success will soon follow. Beliefs are like a pair of tinted glasses you wear, and most importantly change. Instead of the blinkered and limiting glasses you currently wear, why not try on a more optimistic pair to see how it feels? Surely then there will be some kind of lift-off, you will suddenly lose weight, have amazing sex, become enlightened, happy, and financially free.

Here beliefs are in your head acting as some pre-perceptual filter altering and organising your experiences. However, success isn’t just about changing your beliefs. You live in a society where outcomes depend on others’ actions, attitudes, and structural constraints. Changing your beliefs without the work of changing other’s beliefs about you is just a recipe for disappointment.

There are two reasons. Firstly, the thesis doesn’t account for scarcity. The kinds of positions in society that are desirable are fewer than the people who want them. If you want to become a bestselling author, you must not only write a fantastic book but also persuade a sizable number of people to read it instead of other books. It will have nothing to do with your beliefs. In other words, you have to change other people’s attitude to you, even if it is in some small way.

Even if we grant that there are many good and successful lives that do not involve being super-rich playboys who drive sports cars and live in mansions, the thesis is still a bad one. You do not exist separately; you live in a community. The community I mean is a specific philosophical one. It’s not some cosy village, but a highly specific community of subjects who give and accept reasons. We give reasons for behaviours such as eating certain foods or pursuing certain goals.

That is, we must justify ourselves to each other.

It is not just a case of changing behaviour and sticking to a diet. You must also change the attitudes of everyone in your life, because the weight you are is a structural part of the lives that are intertwined with yours. I have a friend who wants to lose weight, but his partner expresses her love through baking. If he cuts back, his marriage suffers. His weight isn’t merely a belief he has, but something which is the outcome of a process he isn’t in control of. The beliefs he has about his body are a structural part of his way of life. He will have to change much more than just his beliefs.

As a result of living in these communities, people will treat you in certain ways because of what they think of you. There will be some actions you cannot take and some lives will be completely foreclosed from you. What you can achieve depends heavily on how others perceive and treat you.

All of this is a roundabout way of saying that you simply cannot change your beliefs to create the outcome in the world that you want. If it were that simple there would be no need for the mass political movements we have seen over the past 50 years or so.

Instead you have to bring other people along with you—you must change other people’s minds to achieve different things. Changing your mind is easy, changing other people’s minds about you is much harder. Often much harder than just living your current life.

Gay people, for instance, had to convince wider society that they were not mad, and then that they were not diseased. Now that they are an integrated part of society, they are no longer subject to the sort of discrimination that left them careerless and penniless, as many found themselves in previous generations. (Or they just ended up dead because wider society felt that death was the best outcome for them.)

Want to start a business? You have to persuade other people to give you their money. Want to write? You have to persuade others to read you.

There is no action in a vacuum.

entry.title: Two Concepts of Freedom
entry.content:
Freedom[^1] is not the defining value of our age. This is not because freedom lacks importance, but because it has lost material meaning. Freedom is not some Platonic ideal floating in the ether, waiting to be discovered. To mean anything at all, it must structure how people actually live. And freedom has been cannibalised by the current historical moment’s (1979 to the present) obsession with efficiency—specifically, Pareto efficiency.

The ancients understood what it meant to live freely: you were not a slave. Between the fall of the western Roman empire and the Enlightenment, freedom took on a more spiritual dimension. It came to mean acting in accordance with your station in life—what Hegel called the “unhappy consciousness” of scepticism, stoicism and early Christianity.

After the French revolution, freedom acquired substantial meaning. People need not act according to their station in society. They could create their own actions and give themselves meaning. This is the lesson of the spirit sections of Hegel’s “Phenomenology of Spirit”: we realise, through giving and accepting reasons, that our lives are governed by values we took to be natural but which we ourselves created. We could, collectively, act differently and thus change the world.

Two distinctly contemporary meanings of freedom emerged in the 20th century. Both relate to choice.

The first is revolutionary freedom. When the world becomes intolerable, people make an irrevocable choice to live differently and thus change it—through force or example. Think of 20th-century revolutionaries (communist or otherwise) or the gay- and trans-rights movements. These people rejected prevailing society entirely and set out to build something different. Once you have committed your first terrorist act or come out of the closet, there is no going back. In that self-defining act comes a kind of freedom. You need not concern yourself with giving and accepting reasons within a community. No norms structure your life apart from the revolution.

The second is consumer freedom. This conception places consumer choice as paramount. Agents are free to exchange on open markets rationally (that is, in utilitarian terms), so the unimpeded operation of markets is essential. Here there is no structuring norm beyond what each agent values, and no defining act beyond which one cannot return.

Neoliberalism can be defined as the system in which consumer freedom has cannibalised both revolutionary freedom and the post-Enlightenment conception of collective self-determination. We understand freedom today purely as choice. This is a cultural regression. Instead of creating new kinds of people or ushering in new concepts, we are frozen within a single market-based norm.

This is visible everywhere. Being gay or lesbian is no longer a counter-cultural choice. It is not about creating new types of self but one more option for how to be. Sexual practice has been normalised, and with it the meaning of gay freedom has changed. This is why politics cannot progress and why fascism is attractive: fascists promise something new.

We should return to something like revolutionary freedom: finding the world so intolerable that we are forced to change it. We must reject society completely, as the revolutionaries did, to have any hope for the future.

What would this look like? Instead of the “cash in the attic” economy and the “types of guy” approach to living, we need transformation. These ideas are connected: until we learn to become new kinds of people and resist reduction to pure consumer choice, we will never have a new economy.

[^1] I am trying out a more “low effort” approach this year, so strap in!
entry.summary: Freedom[^1] is not the defining value of our age. This is not because freedom lacks importance, but because it has lost material meaning. Freedom is not some Platonic ideal floating in the ether, waiting to be discovered. To mean anything at all, it must structure how people actually live. And freedom has been cannibalised by the current historical moment’s (1979 to the present) obsession with efficiency—specifically, Pareto efficiency.

entry.title: Story Structure is simpler than you think.

link.title: Story Structure is simpler than you think.

entry.content:
I begin every writing session with a sort ten to fifteen minute timed automatic writing exercise. The point is to get some air through my mind. I use a program (flowstate) which deletes what I’ve written if I stop. It helps with not editing.

This little post was the outcome of one of those sessions. It was mostly a reminder for me. It might be more useful for you, I hope it is.

Anyway. Enough with the throat clearing.

What I want to say is that writers overcomplicate story structure. They think there is a single story structure — the One Story Structure — and that their story is Good or Bad by virtue of how well their plots hew to the grand structure. This is further exacerbated by the whole cottage industry of experts and whatevers which promise that as long as their stories follow the mold, then success (of whichever form the writer desires) is soon to follow.

Of course, this is bullshit. Plotting is both simpler and more difficult than simply following some mold. There aren’t 21 steps a protagonist must go through for the story to be valid. That’s a fairy tale for writers — the purpose of which is take away some of the terror of coming up with ‘what happens next and why.’

I say that it’s simpler since we all ‘plot’ all the time—that is we want things, and come up with plans to get them. As we execute those plans we naturally come up against interference, constraints, hazards, or our plans go awry, they backfire on us, and fall through. So, despite the fashion for well crafted sentences and interiority in fiction, we all have a grounding in what makes a dramatic character: intention and obstacle. At base that’s all there is too it, a character wants something and has to navigate around, or through, a series of escalating obstacles, until they definitely have achieved their aim, or definitively have failed. The remainder of the story deals with what that success or failure means for your character. Whether they could do something (e.g. ask their crush out) that they couldn’t at the beginning of the story, or how now they can’t do something they could earlier in the story.

That all sounds simple, because it is, so the difficulty is all in the execution. A story can sound good in summary, but fail to move us because the prose is dull, the scenes confusing, the sequences meandering. In the end all there really is are marks on a page to read, actors on stage reciting lines, or images on screen. The success or failure of the artwork is all about the arrangement of those base elements—there is no platonic form of the story separate from the execution. There is no world beyond the words, the images are not a window into some other place.

Lets take a couple of examples from my recent life.

Just now I was interrupted in writing this essay because my mother wanted me to help set up the sofa bed I’m sleeping on for the next few days. I wanted to keep on writing, but if I want to have a peaceful life over Christmas I had to help my mother. The task was complicated by my mother not knowing how to turn the bed from a sofa into a bed, my brother calling my mother as she was (badly) explaining how to open the bed to me, my mother getting the wrong size sheet twice, my mother getting in my way whilst I try to do what she’s asking of me, and my father interrupting the whole thing because he needed my help pushing a motorbike with a flat battery into the garage. This whole thing was a test of my patience, and a real life example of farce (interruptions, miscommunication). The stakes were suitably low (just keep the peace in a relationship), and the obstacles easy to overcome (don’t lose my temper). At the end I was really the same person I was at the beginning, which in a comedy is no sin.

The other example came a month or so back when my team had to move offices. Our company had agreed to sublet the floor we worked on to a third party, so we needed to pack everything up and move to our new premises. At stake for the company was a big fat pile of rent money—the subtenant had a firm date when they needed to be in the office (their lease was up), and any delay would mean they cancelled the whole thing. At stake for me was that at work I deal with PII data, specifically a cabinet full of the stuff. Only my team is authorised to see the contents, and I can be personally sued if somebody who shouldn’t has access to the documents (even for a little while).

Normally I am a pretty chill guy at work. I am want to just let things play out as they play out, taking the view that most squabbles are small fry in the grand scheme of things. Being told I needed to move office was just another thing I needed to manage. There was a deadline however: we had to be out by Friday 14th, because on Monday 17th one of our rooms was going to be used for a delicate negotiation involving an external mediator. We didn’t want the process to be interrupted by the chaos of moving.

At first we resisted moving: the new space wasn’t secure. There’s some rather dull legal chicanery we did to force our company to give us a properly specced space. Very quickly, since a lot of money was on the line, the company relented and found a suitable space for us. This included a new lockable room, with brand new keys, that only my team could access (this part is important). So we agreed to move.

In fact, we didn’t do anything as passive as just agreeing to move. Instead we made a plan. My team would pack everything in our office, and the Workplace management would move the boxes on Friday 14th. For the cabinet full of PII data, we would pack them into specially marked boxes, which would be placed in the lockable room, and one of us (me) would accompany them from the old office to the new room and physically lock them over the weekend. We’d move the cabinet at 5pm on the Friday, as it was the very last thing which needed to be moved and we didn’t need to fill it up straight away. Then once everything had been moved, my team and Workplace would do a key handover. They take the keys to the old office and we’d get the keys to the new place. Plus we’d do a load of paperwork to record which keys were where and why. Simple.

The first obstacle was that my team hadn’t sorted what was in the cabinet as the years had gone by. Instead we were too busy and just put everything in the inbox tray on the middle shelf, and promptly forgot about it. So, as well as organising the move, I also had to file a year’s worth of paperwork. This tasks wasn’t so bad, but it turned out our company didn’t have moving boxes so everything had to go back into the cabinet once I’d filed it. I had to overcome our collective distractions, and general hatred of paperwork.

Then what went wrong was that the facilities guy got sick, and didn’t install the new locks in time. Obviously there was nothing I could do about that, but there were other facilities guys onsite who could have installed the new locks, but the office heating system had broken so we understandably weren’t the number priority for them. I was left reeling, trying to persuade or cajole the head facilities guy into doing what I needed him to do. Instead I was fobbed off and ignored.

So we made a new plan: hire a moving company, they provide boxes, we pack everything into these shiny boxes, and the moving company moves everything into the secure location. Except that this plan also goes wrong: my company expanded the scope of the removal company. Workplace needs the movers to do more stuff than can fit in an afternoon, so the move has to be postponed until Monday 17th. The day of the negotiations.

So we make a Final Plan: everyone would arrive early with the movers on the 17th and the facilities guy and do the move before the negotiations. The facilities guy would install the new cylinders last thing on the 14th and hand over keys to the new office. We would keep the keys to the old office. Now there are two sets of keys I was responsible for which can go missing.

Of course, the Final Plan Goes Wrong too. It’s a story, so nothing can go smoothly or there’d be nothing to tell.

I arrive early on the Monday morning to find that the moving company isn’t there. Neither was the facilities guy.

I have to find a trolley and moves the important cabinet stuff myself, but I couldn’t lock it securely since the new locks hadn’t been installed. Also the IT dept hadn’t got around to cancelling meetings in the new secured room, and this it has meetings scheduled in it all day. So I have to organise/persuade other teams to move their meetings and sort out some alternatives, so I can lock the door.

Then I need to move the cabinet. But the moving guys have been given other priorities by the company. Finally I have to intervene and ‘be a leader’ to get the cabinet moved, so the cabinet is finally in its new home.

There were several obstacles I had to overcome: the company forcing a move on me, the internal facilities people and their priorities, the moving company and their instructions, seasonal illness. None of these were, in principle, difficult to get through. They just required that I try different tactics out: persuasion, bargaining, cajoling, threatening the whole move, finally directly intervening and asking the moving company to just move the fucking cabinet already. In other words, the project challenged my chill guy self conception. In some small way, I’m better able to stop being a chill guy when I need to get things done.

What the second story has that the first didn’t are: clearer stakes, deadlines, plans, failures, and a protagonist who changes ever so slightly. Both are taken directly from my actual life, both suggest ‘scenes’ and in the second these are grouped into ‘sequences,’ both suggest ‘genre.’

What I want to say is simply: there’s no need to follow a predetermined formula, or have ‘required scenes.’ Nothing will help us against the terror of the blank page. Nothing but intention and obstacle can help us figure out what next.
entry.summary: I begin every writing session with a sort ten to fifteen minute timed automatic writing exercise. The point is to get some air through my mind. I use a program (flowstate) which deletes what I’ve written if I stop. It helps with not editing.

entry.title: Aristotle’s Politics Books 2 & 3
entry.content:
Aristotle opens Book II of the Politics by stating his aim: to identify the best constitution for those capable of living ideally. Since existing constitutions fall short, he proposes to examine both well-governed city-states and theoretical constitutions proposed by philosophers. He begins with a fundamental question: What should citizens share—everything, nothing, or only some things?

In Book II, Aristotle encourages us to study what is deficient and immediately turns to Plato’s Republic and Laws. This sudden pivot introduces a layer of irony, possibly tongue-in-cheek, especially if Aristotle means something different from what he explicitly says. How, then, are we to read him—particularly when he seems to undermine his own arguments? A comparison with his discussion of natural slavery is illuminating: there, he appears to defend slavery by nature, yet his definition renders it impossible to identify a “natural” slave. If we cannot fully trust the Politics, what does that imply about the Ethics, which shares similar assumptions?

Aristotle launches a detailed critique of Plato’s proposals for communal property, wives, and children. His objections are both conceptual and empirical:

  • On unity: Socrates assumes maximum unity is the highest good, but Aristotle argues that this destroys the essence of a city-state. A polis is constituted by diversity; reducing it to complete unity turns it first into a household, then into a single individual—undermining its political nature. Just as harmony is not unison, and rhythm is not a single beat, excessive unity obliterates what it aims to perfect.

  • On communal property and relationships: Aristotle attacks the logic and practicality of Plato’s model. Logically, Socrates equivocates on the term “all”—collective ownership by “all” does not translate into individual ownership, resulting in a lack of personal responsibility. Empirically, what is held in common tends to be neglected. “A thousand parents” means no real parents; affection and care arise from personal ownership. Furthermore, private property fosters virtues like generosity and temperance. Historically, such communal arrangements are not new—and if they were effective, they wouldn’t have been abandoned. Practically, Plato’s system is unworkable: who manages households if both women and property are shared? And how can farmers be taxed while denied political rights?

  • On happiness and the guardian class: Aristotle identifies a fatal contradiction—if the guardians, who lack private property and families, cannot be happy, how can the polis be happy as a whole? Happiness, unlike mathematical properties, cannot exist in the whole unless it exists in the parts.

Plato’s Laws offers a more realistic constitution, yet Aristotle finds it similarly flawed. Though it claims to blend democracy and monarchy, it in fact leans oligarchic. Its proposed citizen body (5,040) would require a territory as vast as Babylon. The constitution fails to regulate population growth, offers a vague standard for wealth (”live temperately”), and introduces flawed election procedures vulnerable to manipulation by small groups. The result is a constitution that is at once overly idealistic and insufficiently practical.

Turning to other theorists, Aristotle critiques Phaleas of Chalcedon, who proposes property equality as the solution to political conflict. Aristotle’s response marks a shift toward deeper empiricism. Economic equality addresses only one source of faction: people still resent unequal honors. More crucially, injustice arises not only from need but also from the pursuit of pleasure and excess. No one becomes a tyrant just to avoid poverty—they do so for power and luxury. Aristotle argues the real solution lies not in leveling property, but in educating desires. Yet even education may fail to overcome human greed, which tends to inflate needs over time. Phaleas also overlooks military and security implications—equalizing land but ignoring slaves, livestock, or movable wealth creates more problems than it solves.

Hippodamus of Miletus proposes a tripartite citizenry—craftsmen, farmers, and warriors—with corresponding land divisions. Aristotle critiques this as internally inconsistent. If only warriors govern, the other classes become politically disenfranchised, resembling slaves. If warriors must outnumber the others, why include non-warriors at all? His land division creates logistical confusion: who works which land, and how are two households supported per citizen? Hippodamus’s proposed legal reforms (graduated verdicts) are impractical for large juries, and his rewards for innovation would incentivize opportunism and destabilize the regime.

These critiques lead Aristotle to reflect more broadly on legal change. While other sciences improve by revision, laws must balance stability with adaptability. Ancient laws were crude—early Greek bride purchases and naive homicide rules in Cyme testify to this—but laws cannot capture every particular, creating tension between permanence and reform.

Throughout, Aristotle’s method reveals itself: political theory must be grounded in human nature, historical experience, and practical feasibility. He does not reject ideals but insists they be tempered by reality. Humans are naturally diverse, possessive, insatiably desirous, and resentful of both inequality and forced equality. The “best” constitution must be not only logically consistent but also achievable. Education and character formation matter more than institutional design. Crucially, a city-state requires reciprocal equality among diverse citizens—the very multiplicity that Plato’s unity ideal would erase.

The Politics is, in many ways, a strange book. Its naturalism is difficult to take at face value. Aristotle moves between descriptions of “what usually happens” and prescriptions of “what ought to be,” yet the connection between the two is often ambiguous. His teleological method seems to rest on an equivocation: if what is “natural” is simply “what usually occurs,” then there is little room for political idealism. But if it means “what fulfills a purpose,” then the justification must come from something more than observation.

Aristotle is also ironic—he criticizes unrealistic proposals while urging citizens to “be better,” despite his pessimism about human perfectibility. This tension appears in his discussions of property and virtue. Why critique shared property with such weak arguments, unless to subtly signal that the real issue lies elsewhere?

Finally, it’s worth noting that Aristotle assumes a static economy without growth. His discussions of property are, in effect, debates about income distribution. The absence of a growth framework makes his economic assumptions all the more revealing—they reflect a world where redistribution, not expansion, defines political possibility.

In Book III of the Politics, Aristotle shifts his focus to the constitution itself: who should be considered a citizen, what role citizenship plays, and how political community is structured through participation and law. His central concern is to clarify the nature of citizenship, examine the composition of the citizen body, and explore the proper organization of political power. This inquiry is essential for identifying the best achievable constitution, grounded in human nature and practical realities.

Aristotle opens by emphasizing that citizenship is fundamentally defined by participation in the judicial and deliberative functions of the polis. Unlike a modern notion of citizenship as mere residency or legal status, for Aristotle, being a citizen means actively ruling and being ruled in turn. This reciprocity distinguishes citizens from subjects or servants. Importantly, this definition is flexible: the citizen body varies depending on the constitution and its institutions, reflecting different roles and scopes of participation.

This leads Aristotle to a vital methodological point: constitutions must align with the nature of their citizenry. For instance, in oligarchies, the wealthy hold political power, while in democracies, all free males (usually property holders) participate. Aristotle’s approach here balances empirical observation of existing city-states with normative analysis of what political roles best suit different people.

A crucial question arises: who qualifies as a citizen? Aristotle critiques extreme inclusivity and exclusivity alike. He argues that citizens must be free, adult males who share in political power, yet the precise boundaries depend on each city’s customs and laws. This flexibility acknowledges human diversity but also creates ambiguity—an ambiguity Aristotle neither fully resolves nor dismisses.

Aristotle then addresses the composition of the citizen body, emphasizing the need for a balanced and stable polity. He warns against factionalism that arises when wealth, birth, or virtue become the sole criteria for citizenship, as such exclusivity breeds resentment and instability. Instead, he advocates for a middle ground: constitutions that encourage a broad but politically active middle class, capable of mediating between extremes of wealth and poverty. This “golden mean” of political inclusion, Aristotle suggests, supports social cohesion and stability.

Moving to the question of political offices and magistracies, Aristotle insists these should be filled in ways that reflect the constitution’s character and citizen virtues. Selection by election or sortition depends on context; election rewards merit, while sortition preserves equality. Aristotle is wary of concentrating power in a few hands, and his nuanced approach reflects his broader political prudence.

The issue of the rule of law versus rule of individuals also takes center stage. Aristotle champions the rule of law as superior because laws, when well-crafted, embody reason and justice more reliably than fallible rulers. Yet he recognizes that laws must be adaptable and supported by the virtue of citizens and magistrates, revealing his skepticism toward rigid legalism detached from human character.

Aristotle’s treatment of justice in Book III is both technical and practical. He distinguishes between “distributive” and “corrective” justice, grounding political equality in proportion rather than numerical equality. Justice requires giving people their due according to merit, contribution, or need, but Aristotle carefully notes that this proportionality varies with the constitution’s form. For example, in a democracy, equality among citizens might mean equal political voice, while in an oligarchy, it might mean proportional influence by wealth. This approach reveals Aristotle’s pragmatic acceptance of different, context-dependent notions of justice.

The question of regime stability and the prevention of factional strife emerges as a continuous theme. Aristotle identifies multiple sources of conflict—wealth disparity, honor, birth, and power—and insists constitutions must actively address these tensions through balanced citizenship and laws fostering shared interests. He criticizes the tendency of extreme regimes to devolve into tyranny or mob rule, emphasizing moderation and mixed constitutions as ideal solutions.

Throughout Book III, Aristotle maintains a tension between ideal political arrangements and what is practically achievable. Like in Book II, he balances teleological reasoning (what a polis ought to be) with empirical observation (what actually exists). His prescriptions are deeply shaped by assumptions about human nature: humans are political animals capable of virtue but also prone to faction, envy, and ambition.

Aristotle’s irony and ambivalence appear again. He promotes broad political participation yet excludes women, slaves, and many resident aliens from citizenship without fully explaining why this exclusion is just or necessary. His emphasis on reciprocity and mutual rule raises questions about the limits of inclusion and the ideal scope of political community.

Finally, Book III implicitly acknowledges the limits of political theory itself. The variability in constitutions and citizen definitions reflects the complexity of human societies. Aristotle’s method is therefore neither rigid blueprint nor idealistic fantasy but a practical framework that encourages adaptation, balance, and education to foster the polis’s flourishing.

entry.title: Aristotle’s Politics, Book 1
entry.content:
The Politics was a sequel to the Nicomanchean Ethics; or rather, they were all one treatise. The Ethics concerned itself with how an individual could achieve eudaimonia, the Politics was which institutions could even allow an individual to achieve eudaimonia. One can therefore see the Ethics as a sort of applied politics, whereas we moderns see Politics as applied Ethics.

Continuing on the theme of reading the Politics in relation to the entire extant Corpus of Aristotle—it’s important to keep in mind that Aristotle was a naturalist (for example he wrote a lot about fish). The Politics/Ethics is to be taken as an extension of this attitude: the argumentation has a ‘let’s look at these examples’ quality. There is no poetry, and nobody becomes Aristotle’s patsy at the end of a dialogue. Because he was so interested in nature Aristotle led a peripatetic life. Yet he always returned to Athens. The ideal Polis of the Politics is Athens. As such the book serves as a simultaneous description and legitimation of Athens.

Intersubjectivity through language is what makes us rational. Aristotle makes some off-hand comments connecting rationality and speech—this is the faculty which allows us to know good from bad. It’s clear he sees intersubjectivity through language as a defining feature of humanity. The Politics lays out arguments for who can be rational in Aristotle’s sense (it’s clear slaves will never be).

The book is about communal life, but without a modern state. There is no Leviathan in Aristotle’s world-picture. The state is something else entirely. The implication for us is that the citizens of the Polis are still in the state of nature, and as such any political benefits they have they have naturally. There are two things I want to say about naturalness so far as described in the Politics. The first is that in the Physics Aristotle introduces “the idea that the natural is that which occurs always or for the most part. The main Physics discussion, which revolves around the idea of an internal source of changing or being changed, does not discuss this, but it emerges slightly later. Something is natural or by nature if, starting from some internal principle, it develops continuously ‘always something going towards the same thing, if nothing interferes.[^1] Thus the natural is the usual.” In chapters 8-11 however Aristotle uses a separate conception of the natural: the conclusion of Chapter 8 argument on wealth building is that the only form of natural money-making is in obtaining and managing the store of necessary and useful goods (from farming, hunting, herding, etc.) needed for self-sufficiency and the good life, which has an inherent limit determined by the needs of household management. Here Aristotle is using a concept of the natural not as ‘the usual’ but as ‘the ideal.’ I feel that throughout this book (especially on the section on slavery) he equivocates between the two conceptions.

In Nature, Justice, and Rights in Aristotle’s Politics Fred D. Miller, J ‘distinguishes two senses of a natural right:

  1. natural right is based on natural justice
  2. a natural right is possessed in a state of nature, i.e., in a pre-political state (his emphases).

He points out that someone may possess natural political rights (1) without possessing any natural right (2). How Aristotle’s conception of natural rights differs from those of Hobbes and Locke. Locke endorses natural rights in both senses, Hobbes in the second sense only, and Aristotle only in the first sense. That is to say, Locke argues that under the law of nature, we possess natural rights in the state of nature, and that the law of nature also serves as a moral foundation for a political contract (119-20). Hobbes argues that in the state of nature, we possess an unrestricted natural right of liberty, and that by the laws of nature we accept restrictions on his right with a political contract (117-19). But Aristotle offers a concept of natural rights which is not “pre-political.” His conception of natural justice presupposes a political constitution; it “is understood as inherently political” (122-23). It is hardly surprising that natural rights are political for Aristotle, as he ass human beings are political animals.’ I can see how the natural rights crowd falls in love with Aristotle: when you have never left the state of nature, then everything is natural. Philosophers are provided with a natural grounding or justification for whatever they want.

I see Aristotle as making four arguments in Book 1:

  1. An argument for the Naturalness of the Polis.
  2. An argument around Slavery and different types of rule.
  3. An argument about wealth and household management.
  4. An argument about virtue.

Basically I read it as (1.) providing a framework for (2.). (2.) establishes the following proposition (which is never all that clearly stated):

  • Different kinds of people exists naturally

And this proposition justifies the following:

  • There are different, and differently appropriate, types of rule.

These propositions are then applied to (3.) and (4.) to justify a kind of constitutional pluralism (which is the project of one of the other books).

There are two very puzzling arguments which didn’t seem, on the first reading, to me to support the constitutional pluralism thesis. I didn’t understand why he spent so much time on slavery and household management. In fact, (2.) and (3.) make up the bulk of Book I (chapters 3-7 are on slavery and 8-11 are on household management).

Further Book 1 is divided into two broad discussions: 1-2 followed by 3-11, and the puzzle is how they are connected [^2]. In chapters 1-2 Aristode asserts:

  1. A plurality of types of rule at 1.1 1252a9-17
  2. That the parts (in some sense) of the polis are households at 1.2 1253bl,
  3. That the city, and the households that make up a city, and the relationships that make up the households are natural (in some sense) at 1.2 1252b30-2.

Are these discussions connected, or are they separate? And if they are separate, why include a discussion (3-11) which doesn’t casually support the argument?

It seems to me that one way of seeing it is that these were lecture notes between a teacher and his students, not something which had been prepared for publication. So the two discussions might actually be separate discussions, say as part of a long digression in a question and answer format. We can never really rule it out, as on a textual level the extant works of Aristotle seem very loose and full of gaps. I will comment on another one below.

We could say that the household management discussion is there because, even though it’s a subject distinct from politics, we have to discuss households simply because the polis is composed of households (from Aristotle’s imaginary natural history of the Polis) and so we need to account for how households can be run. But that just begs another question: why do we need to account for the parts to account for the whole? Simply because how the parts are governed will tell us something about how the whole is governed (because since the households are for the Polis, teleologically speaking, analysing them will tell us about the Polis). Another way of seeing it is that discussion of household management is there because Aristotle wants to establish something—namely that there are different types of political rule. That is the ‘project’ of Book I as I see it, and parts of the rest of the book will mirror Aristotle’s arguments elsewhere about means between deficiencies and extremes.

The discussion in chapters 3-7 and 8-11 are still quite mysterious. They don’t casually support what Aristotle seems to me to be setting out to achieve. Naively (I am no Aristotle!) it seems to me to be easier to directly assert that there are different kinds of people and this would require different types of rule. I suppose here he is responding to some intercooler (Plato? Xenophon?) who he doesn’t explicitly name. The two arguments have a parallel structure: both seem to reject what might be called a technocratic view (in slavery that ruling is a science which is the same in all contexts, and all that differs is the number of subjects; in wealth management that wealth is unlimited and money is the end and accumulation the goal) in favour of a more holistic view point (from slavery we find that ruling requires character and it is different in kind when the nature of the ruled differs; from wealth management that wealth has some limit and that the good life is the end to which accumulation is only the means). Both arguments follow a pattern of rejecting a reduction, affirming plurality, and grounding the practical life in teleology.

The argument for Constitutional pluralism comes from the slavery and virtue discussions (Chapters 3-7, 12-13), not the wealth chapters. Chapter 5-7 establish three natural relations:

  • Master/slave corresponds with Despotic rule
  • Father/children corresponds with Monarchical rule
  • Husband/wife corresponds with Constitutional rule

And Chapters 12-13 establish different deliberative capacities:

  • Slave: missing entirely
  • Woman: lacks authority
  • Child: incomplete
  • Free man: complete

The section on household and wealth management seems to added for a kind of thematic coherence:

Topic 1: Types of Rule

  • Against: One science fits all contexts
  • For: Different natural relations require different rule

Topic 2: Slavery

  • Against: All slavery is conventional/unjust
  • For: Some slavery is natural/just

Topic 3: Wealth

  • Against: Unlimited accumulation is household management
  • For: Limited acquisition for good life is natural

The common thread is that natural teleology grounds proper limits and appropriate diversity. Aristotle seems to be trying to thread a needle where he establishes a (pretty loose) framework where diversity (in peoples and constitutions) exist and this diversity has normative implications, which means that we need to reject technical and univocal solutions.

However, this whole discussion hinges on the naturalness of slavery. Unlike wealth management, which was a thematic addition, slavery is part of the direct chain from naturalness to constitutional plurality. The argument for slavery seems to me to go through four phases: definition and controversy (Ch. 3-4), a defense through natural hierarchy (Ch. 5), addressing objections (Ch. 6), and then distinguishing types of rule (Ch. 7).

In stage 1 Aristotle introduces two views, the first is that mastership is a science, and the second that slavery is unnatural. He ends by concluding that natural slaves exists, and defines them as animate tools. The second stage justifies natural slavery through types of rule: firstly, the ruler/ruled relationship is natural and beneficial; secondly the soul rules the body, whilst reason rules emotion; thirdly those who differ as body/soul or beast/human are natural slaves; fourthly nature tends (but often fails) to make bodies match. Aristotle then answers some objections: that nature often fails, but natural slavery still exists in some cases; and that natural slavery involves mutual benefit; legal slavery doesn’t. Finally in the fourth stage 4 Aristotle concludes that the Master is the Master by character, and that there are different ways (mastership, statesmanship, household management, and kingship) of ruling.

Honestly, I don’t think this is a persuasive argument. It seems to bake its conclusions into its premises. Every major claim in Book 1 is asserted, not argued: the master/slave relation is natural, non-Greeks are naturally slavish, men naturally superior to women (no argument), different people have different deliberative capacities. It seems to me that you will end up at natural slavery if that’s where you start. I’ll lay my ideological cards out on the table here: I’m a Quaker and I don’t think that slavery is just. There’s apparently been a lot of back and forth in the literature about whether Aristotle could have meant something coherent, not whether what he actually wrote is valid.

There are a few objections however.

  1. Across the Ethics and the Politics Aristotle makes conflicting remarks[^3] about slavery. In the Ethics VIII 10-11, Aristotle characterizes the master-slave relationship as tyrannical since it serves the master’s advantage rather than the slave’s. In a tyrannical relationship there is little justice and no friendship. Here in the Politics Aristotle is arguing that some people are natural slaves by nature and that slavery is both just and beneficial for them. Natural slavery is the centrist middle ground between those who justified all ancient institutions of slavery and those who opposed slavery entirely as contrary to nature. Since Aristotle intended the two lecture series to be co-terminus, it’s difficult to know what to make of this.

  2. The conditions of natural slavery seem incredibly high to meet[^4]: the slave must differ from the master “as much as soul from body and man from beast” and he slave must be human enough to be useful but bestial enough to deserve despotic rule.

  3. Similarly the definition is illogical[^5]: what justifies enslavement (being beast-like) is eliminated by enslavement (receiving reason).

It seems to me that we don’t have to think too hard about this argument: it’s clear that the purpose of Book I was to go from different types of people, through different types of rule, all the way to constitutional pluralism. Aristotle would have been primarily responding to Plato, especially his ethical and political monism. We could say something like, it would have been simply unimaginable for Aristotle to conceive of an economy without slaves, but it seems that other Greeks disagreed. Alcidamas (a pupil of Gorgias) said in the Messeniakos “God has set all men free; nature has made no man a slave.” Slavery was obviously controversial: Aristotle spends chapters 3-7 on slavery and explicitly introduces objections up front in chapter 3, and he goes further he defends slavery. Either straightforwardly, or as a stepping stone to some larger and more sophisticated point.

I guess my broader point here goes something like: why is Aristotle still on the syllabus? I have never felt that the Greeks were the spring from which I originate intellectually. They have always seemed a remote and alien people, and the Romans hardly better. There is little glory to be regained squabbling over rocks or dusty papers.

[^1] Annas, Julia. “Aristotle’s” Politics”: A Symposium: Aristotle on Human Nature and Political Virtue.” The Review of Metaphysics (1996): 731-753.

[^2] Deslauriers, Marguerite. “The Argument of Aristotle’s” Politics” 1.” Phoenix (2006): 48-69.

[^3] Ross, Donald L. “Aristotle’s Ambivalence on Slavery.” Hermathena 184 (2008): 53-67.

[^4] Ambler, Wayne. “Aristotle on nature and politics: The case of slavery.” Political Theory 15.3 (1987): 390-410

[^5] Smith, Nicholas D. “Aristotle’s theory of natural slavery.” Phoenix 37.2 (1983): 109-122.

entry.title: I watched (nearly) all of Paul Thomas Anderson’s films and this is what I learned

link.title: I watched (nearly) all of Paul Thomas Anderson’s films and this is what I learned

entry.content:
This week a new PT Anderson film comes out. To celebrate a local cinema programmed his entire backlog. I had nothing better to do, so I went along. Here are some ordered notes I collected, mostly after midnight. They are raw and unsophisticated and I think pretty good. At least they capture something of the initial rush of seeing new films with new cinematic voices.

  1. Your characters should be alone in frames. If you can’t manage this then characters in the same frame can’t look at each other. This materialises (I can’t think of a better word) the essential loneliness of the American experience. Some good examples:

a. Sydney, with his aged and grizzled face stares directly at John Finnegan in Hard Eight. Sydney’s face fills the frame with an aged concern. When the camera pans to John, he’s looking at the floor. When they get together in a motel after John has assaulted a perp, they don’t look at each other; instead, they look offscreen.

b. Or the opening shot of Punch Drunk Love. Barry is pushed to the edge of the frame, which is mostly empty like his life.

2.Have long shots, long scenes. Have fewer cuts. PTA likes a gynmastic camera. In Boogie Nights there are a lot of shots which float between characters as they sit around a pool and party. We see each characters story, but it’s all one big thing. But more generally, he doesn’t cut that much. There’s no quick fire dialogue between cahracters in the normal shot-reverse shot mode we’ve been tought to become accustomed to. The camera lingers. This has the effect on the body of being slightly medatative, slightly relaxing. But we also can’t look away. We’re forced to look, really look, at the underbelly of American society (in Hard Eight and Boogie Nights especially).

  1. Everyone wants money. They don’t know what to do without it, but when they get it they don’t know what to do with it. “Youv’e got money’ is a constant refrain in Hard Eight. In Boogie Nights everyone has so much money they don’t know what to do with it. It all gets spent on drugs.

  2. At the end of Boogie nights we’re now in the 80s and we find Dirk (originally Eddie) in the same room talking to the same mirror he talked at when he started his porn career in the 70s. He’s about to film his big comeback after a period of drug use. It’s implied that we’ll see all of this again, sometime in the 90s when Dirk has completed another cycle of sex, money, and drugs.

  3. There’s a real movement between Hard Eight, where people are mean and look only for themsevles and Boogie Nights. Here the consequences of their actions are allowed to follow characters.

a. Dirk enters a world of hard partying, starts on soft drugs, ends up taking meth, and in one tight scene his meth-fuelled paranoia tanks his career.

b. Maggie (played by Julianne Moore) has a son offscreen. She never sees him, since her ex-husband has sole custody. When the custody agreement is renewed, she can’t find a lawyer to represent her, or can’t afford one, so she represents herself. But her lifestyle cathces up with her, and her ex gets sole custody. We get to see the aftermath, her crying outside the courthouse, and then snorting a mound of cocaine to numb her distress.

c. Most notoriously The Colnel ends brutalised in prison. He was the main financier (in the 70s) of Jack Horner’s movies, and every time he appears with another precocious girl (none of whom he cares for). Everntually he’s tried and locked up for peadophillia, and everyone who depended on him abandons him to his ignomy.

  1. Money ruins everything, even Jack Horner’s ‘art.’ He starts Boogie Nights looking to elevate porn to the level of art—to make a real film where people ‘stay for the story.’ But time marches on, and video replaces film. To remain solvent Jack has to just push one out one after the other. ‘It is what it is,’ his cameraman and editor tells him. ‘Your films have gotten shit,’ one fan tells Jack. There is nothing that the pursuit of money, no matter how small, will not destroy. We have to live for something else.

  2. Boogie Nights tries to imply that all the porn stars and starlets form some kind of extended Found Family. Everyone has been, in some way, failed and abandoned by their biological, real, parents, and all they have each other. But they cannot really function as a real family: there are no bonds of love and mutual respect and dependency, only an uncesaing appetite to use each other. Late in the film, Jack and Rollergirl head out in a limo looking to entice a college boy into having sex on videotape. The whole episode is horrible and tawdry.

  3. Punch Drunk Love is a satire of sorts. It’s a satire of an Adam Sandler film, starring Adam Sandler. Just that this time Sandler isn’t some puppy looking for love, but a deeply lonely agressive man who’s unable to reach for love, even when it comes literally right up to him. Ultimately, the love interest, Lena, is just a fantasy, becuase all these films are just fantasies, and she’s only there as a catalyst for a small kind of change on the part of Barry. I mean, he doens’t really love her, int he end he leaves her in a hospital after a car accident to go and settle a feud that his own desperation had set in motion. The soundtrack is matches the camerawork; a sort of percussive undertone of anxiety present in every frame.

  4. Sandler is the best part of Punch Drunk Love (I mean a deconstructed Adam Sandler movie wouldn’t work without Adam Sandler), but I think he was in on the joke. You really feel the (passive) agression towards his sisters and the subliminal hatred in Barry. His sisters call him gaylord, and his brothers in law think he’s a failure. And you know what, he is. Barry’s isolation is completely self created, and he festers in it. No wonder he calls a phone sex line instead of going to a shirnk. We can see where Howard Ratner or Danny Meyerowitz came from.

  5. Punch Drunk Love doesn’t really spell out it’s meaning, preferring instead to work through a network of symbols:

a. Colour (red and blue). The very first shot in the film is of Barry Egan in his office. The office is blue, Barry is blue, and he dissappears into the background (helpd by the framing of the shot, where he’s pushed to one corner of the screen). Then there’s Lena and her colour: red. One touch I liked was Barry in the supermarket saying ‘what am I looking for’ whilst a splash of red follows him, out of focus, in the background.

b. The moving van/travel. Love arrives in Barry’s world via a removal van. It’s seen right at the beginning, just after the harmonium is dropped off in his life; it’s seen again after Barry and Lena’s date,

c. The Harmonium. This is the least subtle thing in the film. Initially, Barry can’t play the ‘instrument of harmony.’ At the end he takes it to Lena and plays it.

  1. What’s there to say about There Will Be Blood that hasn’t already been said? It’s just really, really, fucking good. All of PT Anderson’s films have been concerned with how people (reall, how men) live. What was the animated ethos of their life, and how it both drove the forward into glory and then ruin. Boogie Nights had Dirk and his desire for fame, Hard Eight ahd Jon and his desire for money, Punch Drunk Love had Barry and his desire to fade away. There Will Be Blood has Daniel Plainview and his desire to win. This is a fully amoral man, driven by greed. There’s a moment about halfway through the film, the oil well has exploded and Plainview’s son lost his hearing. Plainview has a rictous grin as he stares at the flaming well: he is rich. Richer than his wildest imagination. A colleague asks him if his son will be okay, and Plainview says, plainly, ‘no he won’t.’

  2. The long shots get longer. In this film you really get a sense of the camera purposefully lingering on Daniel Plainview, forcing us to stare, to not flinch and look away. Daniel Day Lewis gives an all time career performance (maybe even the best performance on film). At the end, after he has banished the preacher Eli Sunday, God truly speaks through him.
entry.summary: This week a new PT Anderson film comes out. To celebrate a local cinema programmed his entire backlog. I had nothing better to do, so I went along. Here are some ordered notes I collected, mostly after midnight. They are raw and unsophisticated and I think pretty good. At least they capture something of the initial rush of seeing new films with new cinematic voices.

entry.title: Companies need better Cultures not Better Data

link.title: Companies need better Cultures not Better Data

entry.content:
For the last decade and a half my line of work has been in data. As a way of earning your daily bread, it was mostly ok: data comes in, insights come out. The life of a mercenary statistician had a certain appeal—I thought that there were far worse jobs I could do. For instance, I work in the food space. I don’t grind babies to dust so that I can eat. You could say that the work was morally neutral, but I’d dispute that. Delivering groceries direct to customers cuts the total carbon in the entire supply chain by half. It felt like I was part of something bigger, though typing it out now it’s apparent how needlessly technocratic my motivations were. It wasn’t to help people as people qua people, but to minimise some abstract number.

The passage of the previous paragraph mirrors my experience: from a simple statement of my expectations (‘I turn data into rent money’) through to disillusionment with the ethical basis of what I was doing. I wish that the journey had occurred due to my own enlightenment—that there was some event which totally altered my perception of my work. But there was no moment where it became apparent I had misjudged my vocation, instead I just got bored and frustrated with a few projects.

You see, I was a specialist in A/B testing. What that means is that I helped analysts and product owners at my company design and run experiments on our customer base, mostly in the hope that we can sell people more of our product. One of the truisms of A/B testing is that over 90% of your experiments do nothing. Which means that your current business model really is as good as it gets. The other truism is that experiments are radically uncertain, and all practitioners have to cultivate a level of epistemic openness regarding this. If you truly knew the outcome of an experiment before you ran it, then why did you need to run it?

Alas in the age of machine learning, everything is up for grabs. This includes building ML models which can predict the outcome of experiments. Ok, that was a bit loose. What was claimed about the ML model is that it could predict the outcome metric of an experiment with a ceratin accuracy. As a predictive model it was really good. If we had been using these models to predict the outcome metric they would be fine models. But the idea was to predict the difference in the outcome metric between the test group and the control group in an experiment. This won’t be a good prediction of the actual effect of the intervention because, if the intervention actually has an effect, the test group will be systematically different from the control group in a way which isn’t captured in the training data. Technically, there is a covariate shift, and your model won’t predict well. In other words, you can’t predict the outcome of an experiment. If you want to know what happens you need to run the experiment.

Anyway, this idea consumed three years of my life. Once a powerful VP was convinced that they could predictably shorten experiment run times, then there was no hope of opposing it. It didn’t matter that there were no papers on the subject. It didn’t matter that we’d need 50% more subjects in the experiment to account for the extra uncertainty induced by the ML model. It didn’t matter that it made experiments more difficult to interpret (what do you do if the predictive metric and the underlying metric disagree?) We needed to predict the outcome of experiments before they had concluded.

All this is to say: problems in organisations are political, not technical. They need a political solution. My problem was that powerful executives deemed the time it took to complete an experiment as too long. The business needed to move faster. There were many technical people who saw it as their job to say ‘yes’ to this impulse, and systematically ignore anything which got in the way. Which is to say, companies don’t need better data or engineering. They need better cultures.
